# How Ōkuninushi got its accent back

The ASCII form *okuninushi* is missing something. **Ōkuninushi** restores the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Japanese characters evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the classification logic that separates Tier 1 restorations from Tier 2. By the end, the marks in Ōkuninushi will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Ōkuninushi
- **ASCII form:** okuninushi
- **Meaning:** "Great land master"
- **Domain of influence:** Nation-building, Marriage
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 大国主 (Japanese characters)
- **Live domain:** ōkuninushi.com

## Overview

**Ōkuninushi** (*okuninushi*) — Nation-building, Marriage · Great land master — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Nation-building, Marriage". The name means "Great land master".

Ōkuninushi — the **Great Land-Master** — is the earthly sovereign of Japanese myth: the heir of Susanoo who subdued wild Izumo, built it into a nation with the dwarf-god Sukunabikona, and codified **medicine, agriculture and the rites of marriage**. His was the visible world — **Ashihara no Nakatsukuni**, the Central Land of Reed-Plains — until he ceded it to the heavenly line of Amaterasu in the act of statecraft the chronicles call **kuni-yuzuri**, the transfer of the land.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Ōkuninushi** and serves its temple at [ōkuninushi.com](https://xn--kuninushi-uxb.com). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *okuninushi* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Japanese characters as **大国主**. Etymologically it means "Great land master".

The ASCII form *okuninushi* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Ōkuninushi** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

## The Original Script

The name is written in Japanese characters as **大国主**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *okuninushi* and the PuniCodex restoration **Ōkuninushi** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/oːkɯnʲiɲɯɕi/** — Japanese Reconstruction (Old Japanese Opo-kuni-nusi).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ō-** — from Old Japanese opo-, 'great, large' — the coalesced long vowel the macron preserves
- **-kuni-** — 'land, province, realm' — written 国 in the chronicles, phonetic 久邇 in older spellings
- **-nushi** — 主, 'lord, master, owner' — a standing title in divine names (cf. Kotoshironushi)

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'OH-koo-nee-NOO-shee' — five even morae; the long Ō is a doubled plain O, never an English diphthong; 'shi' is the soft Japanese shibilant.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Japanese** — opo-kuni-nusi, 'great-land-master' — the 8th-century pre-coalescence form attested in the Kojiki
- **Alternate name** — Ōnamuchi-no-kami (大己貴命), 'Great-Name-Possessor' — his second primary name in the Kojiki cycle
- **Folk reading** — Daikoku-sama — the vernacular reading of 大国 that later fused him with the Buddhist Daikokuten

Tier-1: the restoration Ōkuninushi preserves the long vowel (macron Ō) that the ASCII Okuninushi erases — the very feature that marks Ō- 'great' as distinct from a plain o-. One preserved feature, mechanically verifiable: a single-tier Tier-1 name.

## Mythology

Ōkuninushi's cycle, preserved in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), is the longest and most novelistic narrative in Japanese myth — a story of escape, ordeal, sovereignty and renunciation at the meeting-point of earth and heaven.

### The White Hare of Inaba (The First Prescription)

In the Kojiki (Book I), a hare from the isle of Oki tricks the wani sea-beasts into forming a bridge, is flayed for the deception, and meets the eighty cruel brothers of Ōnamuji, who mockingly prescribe a bath in salt sea-water — agony for its wounds. The youngest brother, Ōnamuji (later Ōkuninushi), advises instead a rinse in fresh river water and a roll in the pollen of katami, the cattail rush; the hare is healed. Grateful, the hare prophesies that Ōnamuji — not his eighty brothers — will win the hand of the princess Yakami-hime of Inaba. It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals.

### The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni (The Ordeals Below)

Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land.

### The Dwarf from Across the Sea (Nation-Builders)

While Ōkuninushi labours to order the land, the Kojiki (Book I) tells, a tiny god arrives across the waves in a skiff of kagami pod-husks, wearing the skin of a moth: Sukunabikona, son of the great producer Kamimusubi (the Nihon Shoki variants name Takamimusubi). The two make and consolidate the land together, and devise the arts of medicine and protective magic for gods, men and beasts. When the work is done, Sukunabikona departs for Tokoyo no kuni, the far land beyond the sea, leaving Ōkuninushi to guard the realm they built.

### Kuni-yuzuri — the Transfer of the Land (The Great Abdication)

When Amaterasu resolves that her line shall rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains, the Kojiki (Book I; cf. the Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods scrolls) records that the warrior-god Takemikazuchi is sent to Izumo, where he thrusts his sword into the shore and demands Ōkuninushi's answer. The land-master defers to his sons: Kotoshironushi consents at once, while Ajisuki-takahikone resists and is subdued in a divine wrestling-bout. Ōkuninushi then cedes the land — on terms: a grand palace is to be built for him with pillars raised high and crossbeams thick, and his worship is to be perpetuated by the heavenly line itself. That promised palace is Izumo no Ōyashiro, the Grand Shrine of Izumo, and the treaty-in-myth is remembered as kuni-yuzuri.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Ōkuninushi concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **White hare of Inaba** — His first patient and his prophet: the flayed hare of Cape Keta whose healing proved Ōkuninushi's medicine and foretold his marriage to Yakami-hime; emblem of the province of Inaba.
- **The great shimenawa** — The colossal sacred rope hung across the halls of Izumo-taisha — among the largest in Japan — marking the boundary of his enshrined presence.
- **Susanoo's sword, bow and lute** — The regalia of lordship he carried out of Ne-no-Kuni with Susanoo's blessing — the storm-god's own charter for his rule over the land.
- **The tiny boat of Sukunabikona** — The skiff of Metaplexis pod-husks (ama-no-kagami-no-fune) and the moth-skin cloak of the dwarf-god, emblem of the small partner in nation-building.
- **Herbs and the mortar** — The pharmacology he and Sukunabikona devised for gods and men — beginning with the remedy of fresh water and katami (cattail) pollen prescribed for the hare.
- **The high pillars of Izumo** — The towering hall promised at the kuni-yuzuri, to be raised with pillars 'high as the heaven of the gods' — his eternal seat after the surrender of the land.

## Archaeology & Evidence

Izumo-taisha (Taisha-machi, Izumo, Shimane) is among the oldest and grandest shrines of Japan; the present main hall dates to 1744, but excavations in 2000 uncovered massive clustered pillar bases confirming medieval records of a towering earlier hall — the 'high pillars' the kuni-yuzuri myth demands. The region's cultic antiquity is independently attested by the 1984 Kojindani discovery, a ritual cache of 358 bronze swords, the largest single find of its kind in Japan.

## Across Cultures

Japan's gods met no Roman pantheon; Ōkuninushi's later travels ran through Buddhism instead. Through the folk reading *Daikoku-sama* of the characters 大国, he was identified with **Daikokuten**, the Japanese form of Mahākāla, becoming the smiling god of wealth and the household hearth — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. At Izumo the older identity survived intact: there he remains the great matchmaker of *en-musubi*, the binding of marriage fates, and in the month the rest of Japan calls Kannazuki, 'the godless month', Izumo calls it Kami-ari-zuki — 'the month the gods are here', when the eight million kami convene at his shrine.

Within the Japanese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[fujin|Fūjin]], [[hokkaido|Hokkaidō]], [[honshu|Honshū]], [[jizo|Jizō]], [[kobe|Kōbe]], and [[kyoto|Kyōto]].

## Cultural Legacy

Ōkuninushi still anchors the Izumo region of Shimane, where Izumo-taisha draws millions of pilgrims and couples across Japan pray to him as the nation's matchmaker. The white hare of Inaba endures as the emblem of Tottori prefecture, and his son Kotoshironushi presides over the great pilgrimage shrine of Kotohira in Shikoku. The word *kuni-yuzuri* itself remains the standard term for the peaceful cession of sovereignty — the god's abdication absorbed into the political vocabulary of Japan.

## A Meditation

The Ōkuninushi cycle is a treaty written as myth. The 8th-century mythographers of the Yamato court preserved, almost lovingly, a rival sovereignty — an earth-line descended from Susanoo that owned the visible world — and then sanctified its surrender to the sun-line of Amaterasu. What Ōkuninushi received in exchange is telling: not power but cult, the towering shrine and the empire's perpetual worship. He is therefore the god of everything the heavenly line does not do — healing, farming, matchmaking, the pragmatic order of the reed-plain. Many scholars read the cycle as encoding real negotiations between Yamato and the old Izumo region; whether charter or memory, it makes Ōkuninushi the most humane of sovereigns: a ruler who learned kingship through ordeals beneath the earth, and who gave up his kingdom so that his land — and his god — could endure.

## The Unicode Restoration

Ōkuninushi is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *okuninushi* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 10 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 1: 1 mark of length (Ō). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **ōkuninushi.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--kuninushi-uxb.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees Ōkuninushi; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Japanese characters can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Why This Restoration Matters

The marks in **Ōkuninushi** were never lost; they were only waiting for a carrier that could hold them. Now that the carrier exists, the burden flips: every use of *okuninushi* is a choice to leave evidence on the table. The PuniCodex temple keeps the restored form in circulation — as a domain, a dataset entry, and a scholarly argument — so that the choice to use it stays easy. Accent by accent, macron by macron, that is how the original names come back: not with a single grand gesture, but with a spelling that finally works everywhere.
